title: Femme Fatale
full_review:
In "Femme Fatale" (Warner Bros.) director Brian De Palma brings stylish suspense to his usual tools of the trade -- gratuitous sex and violence. His film-noir thriller features many plot twists as he once again pays homage to Alfred Hitchcock, classic Hollywood "bad girls" -- and himself.

Since Mary Astor in "The Maltese Falcon," Barbara Stanwyck in "Double Indemnity" and Rita Hayworth in "The Lady From Shanghai," legendary Hollywood films have sought to glamorize women who were ruthless and rotten to the core. In this film, Laure Ash (Rebecca Romijn-Stamos) is shaped from the same mold. Like a black widow spider, she uses her feminine wiles to snare her victims into her web, then moves in for the kill.

"Femme Fatale" begins with an elaborate jewel heist gone awry at the Cannes Film Festival, then jumps years ahead to a new story, set in Paris, of a down-and-out photographer (Antonio Banderas) who takes a picture of a woman with a past and unwittingly gets caught in a deadly game of cat and mouse.

As the director takes the audience down a number of atmospheric stairways and corridors full of twists and turns, one hopes that there is a thought-provoking payoff of some kind -- or that the ride itself is the payoff. In all good mysteries, our perceptions about what we thought to be true get shaken up along with the film's guileless patsy, in this case the photographer. "Femme Fatale" loosely ponders the notion that no good deed goes unpunished ... or does it? But in all the film is mostly an excuse to showcase its leading lady's sinewy physique with and without naughty lingerie.

De Palma, ever the visual craftsman, shakes things up and creates layer upon layer of what is real and who is doing what to whom. But ultimately there are too many characterization loose ends and not enough substance to his truncated story.

A more recent generation of filmmakers has unfortunately surpassed De Palma in terms of violence and shock factor, so his trademark endings no longer come as a surprise, even if we still never quite know how things will turn out.

Ultimately, Laure Ash is nothing like the classic Hollywood bad girl in that she is only about her lacy costumes and her seductive techniques. Without them there is nothing at her core to hold us, making the film an empty exercise in voyeurism.

Due to an extended lesbian encounter with nudity, a crude lap dance and striptease, stylized violence and some rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
(
2002
)
